❖Core problem : To represent a curve/surface of any shape.   
❖Line segment-based approximation: 
❖Line segment should be very-very small so that the represented curve looks 
smoother. 
❖ For that, we have to provide sufficiently large no. of points, which we do 
not want.
❖ Curve-based approximation:
❖ We do not have equations for all set of possible curves. 
❖What is desirable?
❖ User can only provide a small no. of (either on curve itself or its nearby points 
called control points) control points, and the system let it interpolate these control 
points to generate the desired curve.

kth –order Spline
▪In general, a given spline is made of piece-wise curve strips.
▪Each strip can be represented by a polynomial of degree K. 
▪For “n+1” no. of control points, there exist “n” no. of spline strips. 
▪So, between each pair of control points, there exist a curve which can be approximated 
with a polynomial of degree K.
▪Follows a continuity of derivatives of order “K-1” at the common joints between segments.

Continuity Condition
❖ Several polynomials are joined together to create a spline. 
❖It is important to ensure that they should join smoothly so that the resulting 
curve (spline) should look smooth.
❖ This is taken care by imposing Continuity Condition at the junctions.

nth order parametric continuity (𝐶𝑛)
❖ nth order parametric continuity (𝐶𝑛)  states that two curve segments (say       
and       )  meet and the 1st  to nth order parametric derivatives of the adjoining 
functions (𝑓· and g · ) are equal at the junction point.
▪(𝐶0; n=0) : indicates that the two adjacent curve segments meet.
▪(𝐶1; n=1) : first order parametric derivatives at the junction point are equal 
▪(𝐶2; n=2) : both first and second order parametric derivatives are equal and 
so on.

❖ Second-order geometric continuity (𝐺2) : states that the tangent direction and 
the curvatures at the junction are equal but their magnitude may differ.

❖Each of the strips is represented by a polynomial of degree 3.
❖So, it follows a continuity of order “TWO” at the common joints between segments. 
Therefor, the generated curve is sufficiently smoother (practical applicability) at the 
junctions.
❖ The low-order polynomial reduces computational requirements (hardware or 
software), and also reduces numerical instability that arises with higher-order spline.
❖It can generate a variety of space curves; however, it may fail to approximate complex 
curves (higher-order spline can be used).
